stem: A client’s continuous glucose monitor shows a near-target mean glucose, but the report also shows frequent excursions above and below the target range and high glucose variability. Which interpretation by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: The mean glucose alone can hide clinically important highs and lows, so time below range, time above range, and glucose variability should also be reviewed before judging control as safe.
options.B: A near-target mean glucose proves the regimen is well balanced even when recurrent hypoglycemia is present.
options.C: Glucose variability has no role in clinical management as long as the A1C or mean glucose appears acceptable.
options.D: Only episodes above the target range matter because fluctuations below the target range do not affect medication safety.

rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care emphasize that A1C and mean glucose do not capture glycemic variability or hypoglycemia and recommend using CGM metrics such as time below range (TBR), time above range (TAR), and coefficient of variation alongside mean glucose. High glucose variability has been associated with hypoglycemia and can signal the need to reevaluate therapy. Therefore a seemingly acceptable average should not be interpreted as safe control when clinically important highs and lows are occurring. B, C, and D ignore safety information contained in CGM pattern metrics.
educational_objective: Interpret CGM beyond the average by reviewing time below range, time above range, and glucose variability so clinically important hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia are not masked by a near-target mean.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
source_document_title: Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_locator: Assessment of Glycemic Status; Glycemic Assessment by A1C — A1C does not measure variability, real-time glucose, or hypoglycemia; Glycemic Assessment by Continuous Glucose Monitoring — TBR and TAR guide treatment adjustment and high coefficient of variation is related to hypoglycemia; Table 6.2 standardized CGM metrics
source_claim_supported: Mean glucose or A1C can mask glycemic variability and hypoglycemia; current ADA guidance recommends interpreting CGM using TBR, TAR, and variability metrics, and high variability is associated with hypoglycemia risk.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential; interpret trends in physiologic monitoring and identify patterns that increase risk from treatment
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — CGM variability and masked hypoglycemia/hyperglycemia
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source broad claim that glycemic variability independently increases ‘complications and symptoms.’ The final item uses the narrower, directly supported ADA 2026 construct: an acceptable average can mask clinically important highs and lows, CGM variability metrics must be reviewed, and high variability is associated with hypoglycemia.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 6. The source explicitly states that A1C does not measure variability/hypoglycemia and that TBR, TAR, and coefficient of variation are clinically actionable CGM metrics.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A is limited to supported interpretation and does not assert that variability independently causes long-term complications. No unsupported variability threshold is needed in the stem.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it prevents false reassurance from an average that masks high and low excursions.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; recurrent hypoglycemia remains clinically important even with an acceptable mean.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; variability is a standardized CGM metric used in management.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; TBR is specifically important for medication safety and hypoglycemia prevention.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A integrates the complete CGM pattern rather than privileging the average alone.
audit_findings.cueing: All options interpret the same CGM report and differ on which metrics should guide safety assessment.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential is appropriate because the construct is recognition of monitoring patterns that increase treatment-related risk.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked long-term-complication overclaim, mean-versus-variability interpretation, TBR/TAR relevance, hypoglycemia association, CV terminology, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
